title: Dutch National Flag Partitioning
summary: Partitioning an array into three buckets around a fixed pivot in one in-place pass using three sweeping markers — the technique quicksort itself borrows to handle duplicate-heavy input.

slides.markdown:
The **Dutch National Flag problem**: given an array containing only 0s, 1s, and 2s, sort it in one pass, in place, using O(1) extra space. Named for Edsger Dijkstra's analogy to the three horizontal bands of the Dutch flag — red, white, blue, each grouped together.

The technique generalizes past exactly three literal values: it's really about partitioning any array into three buckets — less than, equal to, and greater than a fixed pivot — in a single sweep. That generalization is exactly what quicksort implementations use internally to handle arrays with many duplicate values efficiently.

slides.subTitle: low, mid, and high sweeping toward each other
slides.markdown:
The algorithm maintains three index variables: `low`, `mid`, and `high`. `low` and `mid` start at index 0; `high` starts at the last index. `mid` sweeps forward through the array, examining one element at a time, while `low` and `high` mark the current boundaries of the region still to be resolved.

At each step, `arr[mid]` is exactly one of the three values, and each case triggers a different action: a 0 gets swapped toward the front (advancing `low` and `mid`), a 1 is already in its correct region (just advance `mid`), and a 2 gets swapped toward the back (pulling in `high`, but — critically — not advancing `mid` yet).

slides.subTitle: Before low is 0, between low and mid is 1, after high is 2
slides.markdown:
![Array split into four zones by low, mid, and high pointers: settled 0s, settled 1s, unprocessed, and settled 2s](assets/dutch-flag-invariant.svg)

The whole algorithm is one invariant, maintained after every single step: everything before `low` is a settled 0, everything from `low` to `mid-1` is a settled 1, everything from `mid` to `high` is still unprocessed, and everything after `high` is a settled 2. The algorithm terminates when `mid` passes `high`, meaning the unprocessed zone has shrunk to nothing.

assets.alt: Array split into four zones by low, mid, and high pointers: settled 0s, settled 1s, unprocessed, and settled 2s

slides.sectionTitle: Why low/high swaps differ from mid swaps
slides.markdown:
When `arr[mid] == 1`, it's already correctly placed relative to the invariant — just advance `mid`, no swap needed at all.

When `arr[mid] == 0`, swap `arr[mid]` with `arr[low]`. The value coming back from `low` is guaranteed to be a 1 (by the invariant — everything from `low` to `mid-1` is already a settled 1), so it's now safe to advance **both** `low` and `mid`.

When `arr[mid] == 2`, swap `arr[mid]` with `arr[high]`. Here's the asymmetry: the value coming back from `high` is completely unknown — it's from the unprocessed zone, and could be a 0, 1, or 2. So `mid` must **not** advance yet; it needs to examine that swapped-in value on the next iteration. Only `high` moves inward.

```python
def dutch_flag_sort(arr):
    low, mid, high = 0, 0, len(arr) - 1
    while mid <= high:
        if arr[mid] == 0:
            arr[low], arr[mid] = arr[mid], arr[low]
            low += 1
            mid += 1
        elif arr[mid] == 1:
            mid += 1
        else:  # arr[mid] == 2
            arr[mid], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[mid]
            high -= 1
            # mid does NOT advance here
```

`mid` advances on every iteration except the swap-with-`high` case, and the loop runs until `mid` and `high` cross — each element is examined a bounded number of times (at most twice: once as `arr[mid]`, and possibly again after a swap from `high`), so the whole algorithm is O(n) time, O(1) space.

| Approach | Time | Space | Passes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Count 0s/1s/2s, then overwrite the array | O(n) | O(1) | 2 (count, then rewrite) |
| Dutch flag: three markers, one sweep | O(n) | O(1) | 1 |

Both hit the same Big-O — this is a case where the interview value is in the mechanism, not the asymptotics. Counting-then-rewriting is simpler to reason about and a perfectly valid answer; the Dutch-flag version is what's specifically being tested when an interviewer says "in one pass" — it demonstrates you can maintain three simultaneous invariants without a second traversal.

The single most common bug: writing `mid += 1` unconditionally after every branch, including the swap-with-`high` case. That breaks the invariant, because the value just swapped in from `high` hasn't been checked yet — if it happens to be a 0 or another 2, skipping past it without examining it leaves the array incorrectly partitioned, and the bug won't always show up on small test cases where it happens to work out by luck.

The rule to hold onto: `mid` advances when you've just confirmed what's at `mid` (the 1 case) or when the value you swapped in from `low` is already known-safe (the invariant guarantees it's a 1). `mid` does **not** advance when the value swapped in is unknown — which is exactly and only the `high` swap.

Trace on `[2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1]` (`low=mid=0, high=5`):

```
[2,0,1,2,0,1]  mid=0 sees 2 -> swap(mid,high) -> [1,0,1,2,0,2]  high=4, mid stays 0
[1,0,1,2,0,2]  mid=0 sees 1 -> mid=1
[1,0,1,2,0,2]  mid=1 sees 0 -> swap(low,mid) -> [0,1,1,2,0,2]  low=1, mid=2
[0,1,1,2,0,2]  mid=2 sees 1 -> mid=3
[0,1,1,2,0,2]  mid=3 sees 2 -> swap(mid,high) -> [0,1,1,0,2,2]  high=3, mid stays 3
[0,1,1,0,2,2]  mid=3 sees 0 -> swap(low,mid) -> [0,0,1,1,2,2]  low=2, mid=4
mid=4 > high=3, done: [0,0,1,1,2,2]
```

Walking through this by hand on paper (rather than trusting a written trace) is the fastest way to internalize why `mid` freezes on a `high` swap but not on a `low` swap — the asymmetry is easy to state and easy to forget under interview pressure until you've traced it yourself at least once.

The technique isn't actually about the literal values 0, 1, 2 — it's about partitioning any array into three buckets relative to a **fixed pivot value**: less-than, equal-to, and greater-than. Replace "0" with "less than pivot", "1" with "equal to pivot", and "2" with "greater than pivot", and the exact same three-marker algorithm partitions an array of arbitrary numbers around any chosen pivot in one pass.

This generalization is the real value of learning the 0/1/2 version first: it's a clean, minimal case that makes the invariant easy to state, and once it's internalized, the pivot-based version requires no new algorithm — only swapping the comparison `arr[mid] == 0` for `arr[mid] < pivot`, and similarly for the other two branches.

slides.sectionTitle: The same trick lives inside quicksort
slides.markdown:
Standard two-way quicksort partitioning (elements less than the pivot on one side, greater-or-equal on the other) degrades badly on arrays with many duplicate values equal to the pivot — every duplicate ends up on the same side, and repeated partitioning on an already-mostly-equal array can push quicksort toward its O(n²) worst case.

The fix used in production-quality quicksort implementations (Bentley-McIlroy 3-way partitioning, and Java's `Arrays.sort` for primitives) is exactly this three-way partition: split into less-than, equal-to, and greater-than the pivot in one pass, then recurse only on the less-than and greater-than regions — the equal-to region is already in its final sorted position and needs no further work. On an array that's mostly duplicates, this turns what would be quadratic recursion into close to linear time.

The Dutch-flag partition does not preserve the relative order of equal elements — swapping unconditionally moves elements around without regard to their original position, so two elements that were both 1s (or both equal to the pivot) can end up in a different relative order than they started in.

For the classic "sort an array of 0/1/2" problem this is irrelevant, since the elements are indistinguishable duplicates. It matters the moment each element carries associated data beyond the value being partitioned on — sorting a list of (color, item) pairs where you need items of the same color to keep their original relative order (a common real requirement, e.g. maintaining insertion order within a priority tier) requires an explicitly **stable** partition, which this technique does not provide without modification.

slides.sectionTitle: Reaching for a two-way partition on a three-way problem
slides.markdown:
A subtler mistake than the `mid`-advancing bug: applying a standard two-pointer partition (one pointer from each end, swapping to separate "small" from "large") to a problem that actually has three distinct buckets. A two-way partition has no way to represent an "equal" region distinctly from whichever side it gets folded into — it either merges the equal bucket into the less-than side or the greater-than side, silently changing the problem from "three groups" to "two groups with one arbitrarily absorbed."

For plain 0/1/2 sorting this usually still produces a technically-sorted array (any consistent ordering works), which is exactly why the bug can slip through casual testing. It becomes visibly wrong the moment the problem needs the three groups distinguished afterward — e.g., returning the count or the index range of each of the three buckets — and a two-way partition simply has no boundary marking where the middle group starts and ends.
